extracted.intended_audience: users of the Magma computer algebra system (mathematicians, researchers, and programmers performing number-theoretic and polynomial computations)
extracted.subtask_short: using magma for number theory computations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and formal rules for performing integer modular arithmetic, primality testing, integer factorization, residue class rings, and univariate polynomial operations in Magma. Covers function semantics, required input conditions, parameter defaults, and algorithm-selection advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chinese remainder system input requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To solve a system a_i x ≡ b_i (mod n_i) use Solution(A,B,N) (synonym ChineseRemainderTheorem) where A = [a1,...,ak], B = [b1,...,bk], N = [n1,...,nk].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The moduli n_i must be pairwise co-prime. Example: A := [5,-7,1]; B := [4,1,3]; N := [13,24,7]; Solution(A,B,N) returns the least positive solution (e.g., 1865).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal constructors in ZZ coincide
rubrics_metrics.description: In the integer ring ZZ, sub and ideal produce the same result when applied to ZZ and a list of generators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructing ideal< Z | 12, 18 > returns the ideal generated by 6. Magma automatically finds a single generator for ideals in ZZ, returned by Generator(I) (e.g., Generator(I) -> 6 which is gcd(12,18)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of ideals in ZZ
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideals of ZZ are infinite (except the zero ideal), so it is impossible to iterate over their elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, sum, product and intersection of two ideals can be computed with +, * and meet; the Parent of elements of an ideal is ZZ rather than the ideal (e.g., Z eq Parent(I!42) returns true).

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating residue class rings
rubrics_metrics.description: A quotient ZZ/nZZ (residue class ring modulo n) can be created as quo< Z | I >, quo< Z | n >, or ResidueClassRing(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When used to create an integer residue class ring, the quo constructor returns only the quotient itself (no homomorphism). Use ResidueClassRing(n) for direct construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modulus and ideals of residue class rings
rubrics_metrics.description: For a residue class ring R, Modulus(R) returns the generator n of the quotient ideal; ideals of R have the same modulus as R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Modulus(Z6) and Modulus(Z6I) both return 6. All subrings of residue class rings are ideals and principal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating ideals inside residue class rings
rubrics_metrics.description: You can create ideals inside residue class rings, e.g., ideal< Z6 | 2 >.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generator(Z6I) returns the generator (e.g., 2) and Set(Z6I) returns its elements (e.g., {0,2,4}).

rubrics_metrics.name: PrimitiveElement / PrimitiveRoot behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: PrimitiveRoot(R) or PrimitiveElement(R) returns an element of R that generates all units multiplicatively, or zero if R has no primitive element or Magma cannot find one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zero is chosen as the sentinel since zero is never primitive. The order of a primitive element equals φ(n); the number of primitive units equals φ(φ(n)). Use IsPrimitive(a) to test primality of the element as a generator.

rubrics_metrics.name: UnitGroup / MultiplicativeGroup returns group + map
rubrics_metrics.description: UnitGroup(R) or MultiplicativeGroup(R) returns an abelian group G isomorphic to the units of R and the map from units of R to G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements of G are group elements (not elements of R); convert back via the preimage operator @@ and the provided map. Example: G, h := UnitGroup(Z38); G.1 @@ h gives a unit in R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use residue class rings as structures when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: If a residue class ring is being used as a structure in its own right (e.g., as coefficient ring for a polynomial ring), construct it with ResidueClassRing and the residue-class operations described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section cross-reference: modular integer operations (Section 20.2.5) are suitable when main objects are integers; use residue-class facilities when the ring itself is primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: IsPrime semantics and algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: IsPrime(n) returns true iff the positive integer n is prime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If n < 25×10^9 a strong pseudoprime test is used; for larger n, a version of the Atkin-Morain elliptic curve primality proving algorithm is used. Both are rigorous. The default is rigorous (exact) unless the user relaxes it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic primality testing (IsProbablePrime / IsPrime Proof:=false)
rubrics_metrics.description: IsProbablePrime(n) (or IsPrime(n : Proof := false)) uses a probabilistic test (Miller–Rabin) which is fast but has a small chance to declare a composite number prime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Output false is always correct (a composite will not be declared prime as false). The default number of bases (iterations) is 20, giving error probability less than 2^-40. Users may set Bases parameter to change iterations. Use this for speed when small risk is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miller–Rabin witness probability and Bases parameter
rubrics_metrics.description: At most 1/4 of random bases fail to witness compositeness for a composite n in Miller–Rabin; repeating k times gives error probability < 4^-k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use IsProbablePrime(n : Bases := k) or IsPrime(n : Proof := false, Bases := k) to control k. The Magma default is 20 bases (error < 2^-40).

rubrics_metrics.name: PrimeCertificate for independent verification
rubrics_metrics.description: PrimeCertificate(n) returns sufficient information to enable independent verification of Magma's primality proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the Handbook for details on certificate contents and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization(n) semantics and return values
rubrics_metrics.description: Factorization(n) attempts complete prime factorization and returns a factorization sequence (prime factors with multiplicities). It may also return sign (1 or -1) and, if unable to completely factorize, a third value containing unfactored composite factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-zero n, first return is factorization of |n|, second is sign. If function cannot finish due to user-set limits, it may return a third sequence of remaining composite factors; test assignment of third variable with 'assigned' before use.

rubrics_metrics.name: General factorization strategy order
rubrics_metrics.description: Factorization applies a sequence of methods: compositeness test, detection of integer power, test for form b^m ± 1 (Cunningham database search), then trial division, Pollard's rho, elliptic curve method (ECM), and finally quadratic sieve (MPQS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parameters for individual algorithms are tuned for a 'general' n; combining methods is recommended for large integers. Each prospective prime factor is then proved prime rigorously unless Proof := false is set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization parameters to control algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Parameters include Proof (rigorous vs probabilistic), Bases (Miller–Rabin bases), TrialDivisionLimit, PollardRhoLimit, ECMLimit, and MPQSLimit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TrialDivisionLimit bounds trial division prime size; PollardRhoLimit bounds iterations; ECMLimit bounds number of elliptic curves; MPQSLimit restricts quadratic sieve to integers with at most that many digits (sieve cannot be applied to very small numbers). Use SetVerbose("Factorization", true) to see algorithm steps and effects of limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cunningham special-case factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Cunningham(b,e,c) uses an intelligent database search to factor integers of the form b^e + c, c = ±1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The database contains many known key factors for such forms and can be spectacularly fast for moderate b and e.

rubrics_metrics.name: TrialDivision defaults and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: TrialDivision(n) attempts to find factors by trial division up to a default bound of 10000, or up to user-specified B via TrialDivision(n,B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trial division usually does not yield complete factorization for large n; a sequence of composite factors may be returned as a second value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pollard's rho defaults and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: PollardRho(n) uses iteration of x^2 + c starting at seed s; default parameters are c = 1, s = 1, k = 8191 iterations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defaults may be changed (PollardRho(n,c,s,k)). Pollard's rho is effective at finding small prime factors; increasing trials can find more factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pollard p−1 method behavior and parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: pMinus1(n) (Pollard's p−1) can find factors p whose p−1 is B-smooth; default smoothness bound is 100000, seed default 2, interval for gcd checks default 100.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: User may change smoothness bound, seed and interval to tune for particular inputs; method is effective when p−1 has only small prime factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: ECM and MPQS applicability and defaults
rubrics_metrics.description: ECM (elliptic curve method) is typically used to find prime factors up to ~25 digits; MPQS (multiple polynomial quadratic sieve) is used to factor products of two primes up to ~45 digits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ECM default options: smoothness 500, increment factor 1.2, curves 10 (ECM(n, s, r, c)). MPQS should only be applied to numbers >25 digits with no small prime factors; for >80 digits it requires substantial time and space. Users wishing to factor very large integers should consult the Handbook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of verbose output for factorization debugging
rubrics_metrics.description: SetVerbose("Factorization", true) will show the sequence of methods applied and timing, helping to diagnose why factorization failed under imposed limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example shows Trial Division, Pollard Rho trials, messages about remaining composites and sieve applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: NextPrime / PreviousPrime semantics and Proof parameter
rubrics_metrics.description: NextPrime(n) returns least prime > n and PreviousPrime(n) returns greatest prime < n; when speed is required set Proof := false to accept probabilistic results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof parameter behaves like IsPrime: when false uses Miller–Rabin with default 20 iterations and returns probable primes; when true returns rigorous primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: PrimeBasis / PrimeDivisors and Divisors functions
rubrics_metrics.description: PrimeBasis (or PrimeDivisors) returns distinct prime divisors of a positive integer; Divisors(n) returns all divisors including 1 and n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divisors can also be applied to a factorization sequence. Examples: PrimeBasis(44442) -> [2,3,823]; Divisors(44442) -> full divisor list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Univariate vs multivariate polynomial ring distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Univariate polynomial rings have one indeterminate and distinct properties from multivariate polynomial rings; a multivariate ring with one indeterminate is not the same as a univariate polynomial ring over the same coefficient ring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Univariate polynomials are represented internally as coefficient vectors [c0,...,cd] and are preferred for computations where univariate behavior is expected; do not mimic multivariate rings by nested univariate rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing univariate polynomial rings and naming indeterminate
rubrics_metrics.description: Use PolynomialRing(R) or PolynomialAlgebra(R) to create a univariate polynomial ring P = R[x]; provide the indeterminate name via generator assignment (e.g., P<x> := PolynomialAlgebra(IntegerRing());).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions CoefficientRing(P) and Rank(P) return the coefficient ring and number of indeterminates respectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for creating polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: Polynomials can be created by algebraic expression in the indeterminate (e.g., x^4 - 5*x^2 + 3*x + 6) or as coefficient lists via P![c0,...,cd] or elt< P | ... >.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coefficient-list method when most coefficients are non-zero (dense); use algebraic-expression method for sparse polynomials with large degree but few non-zero coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Univariate rational function fields and integer ring
rubrics_metrics.description: FieldOfFractions(P) or FunctionField(R) creates the rational function field F over R; IntegerRing(F) returns the polynomial ring P (ring of integers of F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerator(t) and Denominator(t) return numerator and denominator as elements of the integer ring (polynomial ring). Evaluate and inversion behave as expected in the function field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zero polynomial special-case degree
rubrics_metrics.description: The zero polynomial's degree is treated as -1 in Magma (mathematically −∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Zero polynomial has no coefficients or terms; users should include special handling for zero-polynomial cases in routines calling degree/coefficient/term functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate semantics for univariate polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate(f, r) returns value of polynomial f with r substituted for the indeterminate; if r is in the coefficient ring result is in coefficient ring, otherwise result may be coerced into parent's ring if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate accepts substitution values that do not belong to the coefficient ring in some cases (e.g., matrices), as shown in examples where Evaluate returns a matrix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available polynomial operations and meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard operations include Coefficients, Coefficient(f,k), MonomialCoefficient, Degree, Terms, LeadingTerm, LeadingCoefficient, TrailingTerm, TrailingCoefficient, Reductum, Derivative (nth), Evaluate, Quotrem (gives q,r), Quotient, Remainder, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotrem(f,g) returns q and r with f = qg + r and deg(r) < deg(g). Use these operations per usual polynomial-algebra semantics.

rubrics_metrics.name: GCD / LCM availability for polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: GCD and LCM for univariate polynomials are available when the coefficient ring is ZZ, a field, ZZ/pZZ (p prime), a valuation ring, or a polynomial ring over any of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: XGCD (extended GCD) is available only over a field or ZZ/pZZ and returns d,u,v such that d = gcd(f,g) and u*f + v*g = d.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and primitive-part functions for polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: Content(f) returns gcd of coefficients of f; PrimitivePart(f) returns f divided by its content; Contpp(f) returns both content and primitive part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These functions apply to polynomial rings which have a GCD algorithm (e.g., integer coefficients).

rubrics_metrics.name: Norms and sign functions for integer-coefficient polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: AbsoluteValue(f) (or Abs(f)) returns f if leading coefficient positive else -f; Sign(f) returns sign of leading coefficient; SumNorm(f) is sum of coefficients; MaxNorm(f) is max absolute coefficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for heuristics and integer-polynomial arithmetic; example outputs shown in documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization(f) for univariate polynomials: availability and returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Factorization(f) factorizes univariate polynomial f into powers of irreducible factors when the coefficient ring is ZZ, Q, a finite field, residue ring modulo p, an algebraic number field Q(α), a p-adic ring/field, or a rational function field over such rings (except p-adic rings/fields).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Returns a sequence of 2-tuples <factor, multiplicity> representing factorization of the canonical associate f~; second return value is the unit u such that f = u * f~. For integer polynomials associate has positive leading coefficient; for field-coefficient polynomials f~ is monic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization parameter Al for polynomials over finite fields
rubrics_metrics.description: For polynomials over GF(q), Factorization has parameter Al to choose algorithm: 'BerlekampSmall', 'BerlekampLarge', or 'CantorZassenhaus'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default Al is 'BerlekampSmall' if q < 25, else 'BerlekampLarge'. Algorithm choice may greatly affect execution time; examples show large differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: IsIrreducible and squarefree/distinct-degree factorization functions
rubrics_metrics.description: IsIrreducible(f) tests irreducibility; SquareFreeFactorization(f) returns squarefree factorization; DistinctDegreeFactorization(f) for square-free f over a finite field returns degree blocks and the product of degree-d irreducible factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DistinctDegreeFactorization supports a Degree parameter to limit returned degrees. Use these functions in factorization pipelines (e.g., squarefree -> distinct-degree -> equal-degree splitting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynomial discriminant and resultant functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Discriminant(f) and Resultant(f,g) are provided for polynomials over domains (e.g., integers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Resultant(x^10 + 1, x^5 - 2) returns 3125. Use these for algebraic number and elimination computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hensel lifting requirements and behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: HenselLift(f, s, R) lifts a factorization of integer polynomial f modulo a prime p (given as sequence s of factors over ZZ/pZZ) into a factorization modulo p^k, where R is a univariate polynomial ring over ZZ/p^kZZ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inputs: f (univariate integer polynomial), s (sequence of polynomials over ZZ/pZZ that factor f mod p), R (polynomial ring over residue class ring modulo p^k). Returns sequence of polynomials over ZZ/p^kZZ factoring f modulo p^k. Example provided lifting modulo 5 to modulo 5^4 (625).
